1.pericope_label: Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days... in the place where the tree falleth, there it shall be

schools.summary: Delitzsch reports the charitable reading of the first verse together with the Aramaic, Arabic, German and French proverbs gathered around it, notes that the Hebrew says on the face of the waters rather than into them, and then denies that any change of subject occurs at the third verse — as it would if the first were about beneficence — since the argument runs on one track to the sixth: a man cannot know what disaster is coming, because everything follows fixed laws. Ellicott frames the chapter as the preacher's practical turn, reports the popular explanation of the opening figure while conceding it is easier to object to than to improve on, and reads the seven and eight as an indefinite number of one's own ventures.

Gill takes the bread for all necessaries and insists it must be a man's own, applies the seven and eight to successive applicants, and makes the full clouds a lesson in liberality, since they fill again as fast as they empty.

Clarke reads the whole chapter as a treatise on almsgiving: the figure is rice sown on flooded ground, the giving is never to cease while anyone is in distress, and the clouds justify indiscriminate charity, since it is better to relieve a hundred worthless people than to pass by one in real need; on the falling tree he turns to death, which refines nothing and kills no sin. Wesley reads the waters as those on whom a gift seems utterly lost, and finds behind the seven and eight the custom of sending portions from a feast.

Henry supplies both the agricultural and the mercantile figure — bread-corn spared from the family for seed, and a cargo sent as a venture that will not sink — and insists that the bread be honestly got, since giving what is not ours is injury rather than charity.

debates.question: What is the figure of casting bread on the waters?

positions.view: Seed cast on irrigated land, as in Egypt before the Nile subsides; the popular explanation, easier to object to than to improve on.
Rice sown on flooded ground and trodden in by cattle; older versions also read it of giving bread to sailors.
A merchant's venture sent by sea, trusted to the water and certain not to sink.
Charity to those on whom it seems as utterly lost as seed cast into a river, with a slow but certain return.
A charitable reading widely held and richly supported by proverbs, though the argument of the passage does not in fact turn on beneficence.

debates.question: What does the falling tree teach?

positions.view: The fixity of natural law, which man has no power to suspend and whose workings he cannot foresee.
The finality of the state in which a man dies, since death refines nothing, purifies nothing, kills no sin and helps to no glory.

outliers.note: Collects the proverbial afterlife of the verse across four languages, including Voltaire's verse paraphrase advising that benefits be spread magnificently, withheld from nobody however unworthy, and never enquired after.
Concedes of the standard interpretation of the opening figure that it is easier to raise objections to it than to improve on it.

themes: Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days.
Give a portion to seven, and also to eight; for thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth.
If the clouds be full of rain, they empty themselves upon the earth: and if the tree fall toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falleth, there it shall be.

4.pericope_label: He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap... In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand

schools.summary: Delitzsch distinguishes the two kinds of prudence in view, the proverb being aimed not at provident observation guided by experience but at the impossible calculation of coming weather that postpones sowing until the season has passed; he prefers the reading in which two examples of ignorance are given, following Jerome and Luther, and takes tillage as the prototype of all labour. Ellicott states the principle that demanding certainty before acting amounts to not acting, and points out that the wording leaves it undecided whether the fifth verse gives two illustrations of ignorance or only one.

Gill notes that the over-careful man may lose his seedtime altogether, records both the wind and the spirit as possible senses of the disputed word without choosing, and applies the morning sowing to the morning of youth and the morning of prosperity.

Clarke keeps the chapter on charity throughout: the scrupulous investigator lets the genuine case perish while he sifts, such punctilious people seldom do any good, and since a giver cannot know which object is worthiest, God rewards him by his motive rather than by the merit of the person relieved; he also warns that what a man calls scrupulousness may really be love of money. Wesley reads sowing as doing good and reaping as receiving good hereafter, and takes the morning and evening for early and late in all seasons.

debates.question: Does the fifth verse give one example of ignorance or two?

positions.view: Undecided by the wording: either we know neither the way of the wind nor the growth of the bones, or, keeping the rendering spirit, the whole verse concerns the child in the womb.
Two, following Jerome and Luther; the second clause is a shortened comparison meaning ignorance about the growth of the bones.
Both senses are possible and neither need be chosen.
The soul, and how it comes into the child and is united with the body.
The point is not which, but that a man cannot tell why God allowed these particular people to fall into want.

outliers.note: Turns the proverb about watching the wind into an attack on donors who investigate: the punctilious who must sift every case to the bottom seldom do any good and are generally good for nothing, since while they study the clouds others have joined hands with God and kept a poor man alive.
Insists the proverb is not directed against provident observation guided by experience, but only against the impossible calculation of future weather that postpones action indefinitely.

themes: He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap.
As thou knowest not what is the way of the spirit, nor how the bones do grow in the womb of her that is with child: even so thou knowest not the works of God who maketh all.
In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that, or whether they both shall be alike good.

7.pericope_label: Truly the light is sweet, and a pleasant thing it is for the eyes to behold the sun... Therefore remove sorrow from thy heart, and put away evil from thy flesh: for childhood and youth are vanity

schools.summary: Delitzsch corrects two translators who render the connecting particle truly or yes, denies that light here stands for life rather than the light of life in this world, quotes Euripides on the sweetness of seeing the light, and objects to Jerome's renderings in the last verse, since the Hebrew word covers sadness and fretfulness as well as anger and the parallel term is physical rather than ethical. Ellicott would move the chapter division to the ninth verse and argues that the judgment named there can hardly be anything but a future one, given how much of the book complains that retribution does not happen in this life.

Gill runs the sweet light through natural light, prosperity and life, records an older reading making it the light of the law, and takes the charge to the young man as plain advice, of lawful enjoyment or of spiritual gladness.

Clarke observes that a man who does not die violently dies lingeringly and in pain, quotes Ecclesiasticus on remembering one's end, and turns the ninth verse on the reader — go on, take your full swing, but take this with you, that for all these things God will judge you; Wesley reads the darkness as death, tells the young man to deny his eye nothing and then consider his reckoning, and understands the sorrow of the last verse as sensual lust.

Henry makes the sweetness of light an argument, light being the first thing made in the great world as the eye is among the first in the little one, and concludes that because life is sweet to all men we must double our guard lest we love it too well.

debates.question: In what spirit is the young man told to rejoice?

positions.view: Plainly and seriously, of lawful enjoyment or of spiritual gladness.
As a challenge turned back on the reader: go on, take your full swing, but know that God will judge you for all of it.
The tone is not the question; what matters is that the judgment named must be a future one.
The grammar decides only that the preposition marks the joy's proper season rather than its ground.

debates.question: What is to be removed from the heart in the last verse?

positions.view: Not anger, as Jerome had it, but a word covering sadness, moroseness and fretfulness; and the parallel evil is physical harm to the body, not moral indulgence.
Anger, and with it every violent passion.
Sensual lusts, which the writer elegantly calls sorrow because they gratify now and bring intolerable sorrow soon.

outliers.note: Reads the charge to the young man as a dare rather than a permission, telling him to follow the noisy mirth of the fool and the dissipation of the profligate and take his full swing, provided he carries the judgment with him.
Argues that the chapter division would sit better at the ninth verse than where it stands, and that the judgment named there can hardly be understood of anything but a judgment after this life.

themes: Truly the light is sweet, and a pleasant thing it is for the eyes to behold the sun:
But if a man live many years, and rejoice in them all; yet let him remember the days of darkness; for they shall be many. All that cometh is vanity.

Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thine heart, and in the sight of thine eyes: but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment.
Therefore remove sorrow from thy heart, and put away evil from thy flesh: for childhood and youth are vanity.
